growth_story.headline: Thailand's 1990s boom ended in the 1997 crisis; since 1998 income per person has grown 2.3 percent a year, and just 1.8 over the last decade.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person in Thailand grew 5.3 percent a year, carried by manufacturing exports and foreign investment, with part of the boom fuelled by debt. The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis ended it: income per person fell 4.0 percent in 1997 and 8.8 percent in 1998. Since 1998 growth has averaged 2.3 percent a year, as investment stayed low, the manufacturing engine slowed after the 2008 global financial crisis, political instability grew and the workforce began to age. Shocks broke up the era, from the 2009 downturn and the 2011 floods to the pandemic, when income per person fell 6.2 percent in 2020. Income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, but growth slowed to 1.8 percent a year over 2016–2025, from 2.7 in the decade before.

threads.title: A debt-fuelled boom, then a crash
threads.text: In the 1990s foreign investment, industry and exports drove growth, but the World Bank says part of it was fuelled by debt-driven investment. The 1997 crisis brought a deep fall: income per person shrank 4.0 percent in 1997 and 8.8 percent in 1998, and did not pass its 1996 level again until 2002.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank says Thailand's catch-up with high-income countries has gone into reverse since 2019. Yet the data show income per person at its highest level ever in 2025. Both are true: income per person is still rising, at 1.8 percent a year over the last decade, but more slowly than the high-income bar and Thailand's faster neighbours. The data also show a single era since 1998, while the sources describe steps down within it, after the 2008 crisis and again after the pandemic. The decade averages fit that story: 2.7 in 2006–2015, then 1.8.
